title: The Battlefront to Save Tamil
translation_notes: Fresh T1 translation made directly from the pinned Tamil after a complete P0/source review. No pre-existing English translation was consulted.
The repeated Tamil chapter heading at the start of the first extraction unit is represented only in title metadata, not duplicated as body prose.
The page-47/page-48 sentence split after 'எனக்குத்' and the page-48/page-49 personal-name split 'திரு என்.' / 'வி. நடராசன்' are reconstructed as continuous literary units.
The student procession song on page 48 is restored as a two-line refrain from the page-level witness rather than flattened into prose.
The historical distance unit 'கல்' is rendered contextually as miles; the chapter itself later restates the same march distance using 'மைல்'.
The anomalous extracted forms 'முழககங்கள்' and 'நிறுத்தாதற்கு முன்பே' are translated only by their secure contextual functions; no corrected Tamil spelling or replacement source wording is asserted.
The Jagadeesan green-stone-ring anecdote retains the Tamil hearsay/reporting force rather than being promoted to independently verified fact.

T1 preserves the வெறி / பற்று rhetorical argument, the classroom dialogue, the explicit 'my heart rendered justice to me' motif, the thirty-six-year retrospective, and the final pivot from personal memory to all-India politics.

Proper-name spellings, movement terminology, 'இன உணர்ச்சி', 'தமிழர் படை', 'மறியல் அறப்போர்', and other historically/culturally loaded choices remain open for T2 and terminology review rather than being silently normalised during T1.
T2 normalises the identifiable 1938 தமிழர் படை as the Tamil Brigade, makes its two-hundred-mile walking action explicit, and preserves the concrete வீர நடை as a heroic stride.

T2 preserves Alagiri's oratorical images while improving lexical force: வீரங்கொப்பளிக்கும் becomes 'brimming with valour', and the page-47 crescendo is 'The tiger growled! The lion roared! Summer thunder rumbled!'.
T2 resolves classroom பலகை contextually as 'bench', supported by Tamil lexical usage for a board used as a seat; this does not alter the read-only Tamil source.
T2 renders மறியல் அறப்போர் here as daily picketing carried on as a non-violent struggle, preserving both the picketing action and the அறப்போர் register.
T2 retains இன உணர்ச்சி provisionally as 'sense of race' for this chapter; its final corpus-sensitive English remains a dedicated terminology/cultural-audit decision.
T3 completed an English-only literary read and accepted 18 minor fluency revisions only after every candidate was checked back against the pinned Tamil.

T3 deliberately retained source-driven formulations including Fearless Heart, Summer-Thunder Alagiri, the tiger/lion/summer-thunder crescendo, Hindi demon, the frenzy/devotion turn, 'my heart rendered justice to me', the flare/sprout image, the two Tamil bulls becoming corpses in prison, provisional 'sense of race', and the Tamil/green-crescent flags.
Thought-structure audit passes 20/20 major movements with no reordering, omission or invention; the independent English is frozen at this gate before any existing-English comparison.
paragraphs: Pattukkottai Alagirisami, whom Tamils called the "Fearless Heart," marshalled a Tamil Brigade in Tiruchirappalli and led it toward Madras. Among the prominent figures in that march were the venerable Moovalur Ramamirtham Ammaiyar and Manavai Thirumalaisami.

Alagirisami was a whirlwind orator of the Self-Respect Movement. Wanting nothing for himself, he devoted himself entirely to service of the country. The force and precision of Periyar's arguments, the lines brimming with valour in Alagiri's speeches, and the beautiful Tamil of Anna's speeches greatly attracted me.

Alagiri was known as Summer-Thunder Alagiri. A strapping figure. A gait like a king whose head would never bow. A simple life. The news that a Tamil Brigade under his leadership was coming toward Madras was, in those days, revolutionary indeed!

Moovalur Ammaiyar devoted herself to social service and turned that devotion into action through many worthy works. She conducted many widow remarriages and put the ideals of the Self-Respect Movement into practice. She took charge of preparing food and other necessities for the Tamil Brigade all along its route.

Manavai Thirumalaisami, who wrote political ideas in crisp, incisive strokes, was the editor of the weekly Nagarathoothan. When he wrote under the heading "Pen Dance," his pen truly danced! He too served as a commander of the Tamil Brigade.

The Tamil Brigade walked the two hundred miles from Tiruchirappalli to Madras; anti-Hindi supporters all along the route held receptions for it. Congress friends who supported Hindi caused the Brigade many difficulties. They attacked with sticks. They hurled stones. Unshaken by anything, the Tamil Brigade grew larger from town to town and marched with a heroic stride toward Madras.

On a village road, Congress men tied shoes into festoons and tried to humiliate the Tamil Brigade by presenting them as a welcome. When people in the village, stirred by Tamil feeling, moved to untie and throw away those festoons, Alagirisami stopped them. He stood before the festoon and began to speak. People gathered in their thousands. Alagirisami did not stop. He went on speaking.
The tiger growled! The lion roared! Summer thunder rumbled! Alagiri's speech went on for more than two hours.

"We are going to wipe away the stain that is about to fall upon Tamil and the Tamil people. Is this the welcome you Tamils give us? If only you had spread on the ground the shoes you have hung in the sky, each of us could at least put on a pair and walk!" he thundered.

The flood of people roared and surged forward to cut down the festoon. Alagiri stopped them. "Let those who tied it untie it!" he said. Before his long speech had ended, the Congress men ran up to Alagiri, asked his forgiveness, and themselves untied and threw away the festoon they had put up. Not only that: they gave the Tamil Brigade a tea reception and then sent it on its way.

All along that two-hundred-mile stretch, the Tamil Brigade sowed anti-Hindi feeling in even the tiniest villages. I myself stood as an example of how the anti-Hindi cause drew students. Even in my school days I had a special interest in bringing many students together and forming associations—the Children's Reform Association, the Youth Association, and many more! Meetings every week! Speeches on special subjects!

In 1938, every evening I would line up many students and lead a procession through the streets of Tiruvarur. A Tamil flag in my hand! A cart bearing a picture of Rajaji trying to stab Tamil Mother with the dagger called compulsory Hindi! The procession under my leadership! A song I had written; all the students would sing it together:

"Come, everyone, let us go to war!
Let us drive back the Hindi demon that has come!"
That was the refrain of the song.

At that time, a man named Jagadeesan was on a hunger strike in Madras against Hindi. The fast stretched on past sixty, seventy days. Periyar went to see him. It is said that the fasting man told Periyar of his desire for Periyar's green-stone ring. That very day, Periyar announced at a meeting that he had no faith in hunger strikes and such things.
In our student procession, we smashed to pieces the fasting man's picture that I had carried in my hand day after day. By then, he had already ended his fast.

One day, my class Hindi teacher saw our procession. I handed him the leaflet in my hand, filled with anti-Hindi slogans. He took it and went away without a word. The answer to it was waiting in class the next day.

Neither when I handed the leaflet to the Hindi teacher nor when I stood before him holding the Tamil flag and shouting, "Down with Hindi! Long live Tamil!" did I feel the slightest fear. In my bloodstream and in my breath, the feeling "Tamil! Tamil!" kept surging. Some may call that feeling frenzy. If devotion is to be called frenzy, then that meaning is perfectly right!

If proof is needed that love of one's mother tongue rises above everything else, the finest example is this: Mr N. V. Natarajan, who had been working for the Congress Party in Madras's Peddunaickenpet, joined the movement to protect Tamil against the imposition of Hindi. Was it not because of their great love for Tamil that great Tamil scholars such as Maraimalai Adigal—who stood in the opposing camp on the ideas of the Self-Respect Movement—joined Self-Respect leader Periyar in opposing Hindi?

I was of an age, and possessed of a fervour, when every throb of my heart sounded a Tamil melody. I considered even placing an anti-Hindi handbill in the Hindi teacher's hand to be a revolutionary act.
He wrote a few Hindi words on the blackboard in the classroom and ordered me to pronounce them. I stood up.
"Hm! Let's see you read them!" he said.
How could I read when I did not understand them? So I stood silent. He came near. The classroom seemed to be waiting eagerly for something. The teacher twisted my ear.
"Can you read or can't you?" he growled.
"I don't understand," I said.
He slapped me hard across the cheek. My head spun as though the classroom itself were turning. I steadied myself and sat down on the bench. I understood why the teacher had hit me.
"What I did during yesterday's procession was right! What he has done now is right too." Thus my heart rendered justice to me.

All the teachers expected me to gather the students and launch agitations such as a strike against the Hindi teacher! My brain did not work that way. The Hindi teacher himself stayed away from the high school for two or three days. At the gates of Tiruvarur High School too, activists of the Tamil movement carried on daily picketing as a non-violent struggle. I stopped going to Hindi classes.
Thirty-six years have passed since that Hindi teacher struck me. About five years ago, that same Hindi teacher was waiting outside to take me to a homeopathy conference held in Mylapore, Madras.
Now he is no Hindi teacher! He is the head of a large institution that has trained many homeopathic doctors in Tamil Nadu.

When I think that I am one who sprouted from the language struggle that flared up in Tamil Nadu thirty-six years ago, a majestic stride and a proud gaze come over me from somewhere, without my even knowing it!
It was in that very battlefront to save Tamil that the two Tamil bulls Thalamuthu and Natarajan became corpses in prison.

Speaking of compulsory Hindi, Anna said: "Compulsory Hindi became a good opportunity for our sense of race to well up, our sacrifice to become known, truth to emerge, and our labour to bear fruit. Our struggle has shown how many mothers are ready to go to prison for Tamil. It helped reveal the radiance of gems like Thalamuthu and Natarajan, who would give even their lives."

While the language war was going on in Tamil Nadu, Hindu-Muslim riots began to spread in the northern regions. During a tour of East Bengal, Subhas Chandra Bose had to face opposition from Muslims. Muhammad Ali Jinnah, on behalf of the Muslim League, threw down a challenge to the Congress Party. Gandhiji described it as a "declaration of war."

The Muslim League pointed to the injustices inflicted on Muslims and the hardships they suffered in Congress-ruled provinces. The All-India Muslim League raised its voice condemning the compulsory Hindi imposed in Tamil Nadu's schools. In that connection, Muslim League leaders in Tamil Nadu too marched in the anti-Hindi ranks. Anti-Hindi conferences were held with the Tamil flag and the green crescent flag flying together.
